analysis_trace: Trial NCT02174549 is a Phase I dose-escalation study of tirapazamine combined with transarterial embolization (TAE) for liver cancer, now in expansion cohort for neuroendocrine tumors (NET). Primary endpoint is ORR by RECIST; secondary endpoints include ORR by mRECIST and Duration of Response.

Evidence retrieved: Europe PMC search results for tirapazamine HCC TAE (MED/35504436, MED/34041204) and NET liver metastasis TAE studies. No direct results for this specific trial available before cutoff.

Tirapazamine is a hypoxia-activated bioreductive prodrug. Mechanism: selectively toxic to hypoxic tumor cells via DNA damage. Rationale for combining with TAE: embolization induces tumor hypoxia, potentially enhancing tirapazamine activation.

Evidence role assessment: (1) MED/35504436 - Phase I tirapazamine chemoembolization for HCC - indirect_direction, same drug/mechanism but different indication (HCC vs NET), numeric_use_allowed=false; (2) MED/34041204 - Phase I tirapazamine arterial embolization for HCC - indirect_direction, same drug/mechanism but different indication, numeric_use_allowed=false; (3) NET liver metastasis TAE studies (MED/35289113, MED/37587855) - indirect_direction, same indication but different intervention (TAE without tirapazamine), numeric_use_allowed=false.

Population matching: Current cohort is well-differentiated NET with liver-dominant metastases. Historical NET TAE studies show ORR 40-60% with TAE alone. HCC tirapazamine+TAE Phase I showed safety and some efficacy signals but no confirmed ORR data available.

Key uncertainty: No published results for tirapazamine+TAE specifically in NET population before cutoff. Phase I design primarily evaluates safety/dosing, not powered for efficacy. Expansion cohort data not available.

Prediction approach: For ORR endpoints, extrapolate from (a) NET TAE alone ORR ~40-60%, (b) tirapazamine mechanism may add modest benefit or no benefit in this population, (c) Phase I studies typically show variable ORR. Predict ORR 25-45% for RECIST and mRECIST. Duration of response highly uncertain given lack of data, estimate median 6-12 months.

Safety considerations: Tirapazamine known toxicities include muscle cramps, nausea, fatigue, ototoxicity. TAE risks include post-embolization syndrome, liver dysfunction. No unexpected safety signals predicted.

Trial outcome: Likely to meet primary endpoint definition (ORR assessable) but as Phase I, success is primarily safety/tolerability with exploratory efficacy. Classification: uncertain due to lack of outcome data.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT02174549 is a Phase I dose-escalation study of tirapazamine combined with transarterial embolization (TAE) for liver cancer, now in expansion cohort for neuroendocrine tumors (NET). Primary endpoint is ORR by RECIST; secondary endpoints include ORR by mRECIST and Duration of Response.

Evidence retrieved: Europe PMC search results for tirapazamine HCC TAE (MED/35504436, MED/34041204) and NET liver metastasis TAE studies. No direct results for this specific trial available before cutoff.

Tirapazamine is a hypoxia-activated bioreductive prodrug. Mechanism: selectively toxic to hypoxic tumor cells via DNA damage. Rationale for combining with TAE: embolization induces tumor hypoxia, potentially enhancing tirapazamine activation.

Evidence role assessment: (1) MED/35504436 - Phase I tirapazamine chemoembolization for HCC - indirect_direction, same drug/mechanism but different indication (HCC vs NET), numeric_use_allowed=false; (2) MED/34041204 - Phase I tirapazamine arterial embolization for HCC - indirect_direction, same drug/mechanism but different indication, numeric_use_allowed=false; (3) NET liver metastasis TAE studies (MED/35289113, MED/37587855) - indirect_direction, same indication but different intervention (TAE without tirapazamine), numeric_use_allowed=false.

Population matching: Current cohort is well-differentiated NET with liver-dominant metastases. Historical NET TAE studies show ORR 40-60% with TAE alone. HCC tirapazamine+TAE Phase I showed safety and some efficacy signals but no confirmed ORR data available.

Key uncertainty: No published results for tirapazamine+TAE specifically in NET population before cutoff. Phase I design primarily evaluates safety/dosing, not powered for efficacy. Expansion cohort data not available.

Prediction approach: For ORR endpoints, extrapolate from (a) NET TAE alone ORR ~40-60%, (b) tirapazamine mechanism may add modest benefit or no benefit in this population, (c) Phase I studies typically show variable ORR. Predict ORR 25-45% for RECIST and mRECIST. Duration of response highly uncertain given lack of data, estimate median 6-12 months.

Safety considerations: Tirapazamine known toxicities include muscle cramps, nausea, fatigue, ototoxicity. TAE risks include post-embolization syndrome, liver dysfunction. No unexpected safety signals predicted.

Trial outcome: Likely to meet primary endpoint definition (ORR assessable) but as Phase I, success is primarily safety/tolerability with exploratory efficacy. Classification: uncertain due to lack of outcome data.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT02174549 is a Phase I dose-escalation study of tirapazamine combined with transarterial embolization (TAE) for liver cancer, now in expansion cohort for neuroendocrine tumors (NET). Primary endpoint is ORR by RECIST; secondary endpoints include ORR by mRECIST and Duration of Response.

Evidence retrieved: Europe PMC search results for tirapazamine HCC TAE (MED/35504436, MED/34041204) and NET liver metastasis TAE studies. No direct results for this specific trial available before cutoff.

Tirapazamine is a hypoxia-activated bioreductive prodrug. Mechanism: selectively toxic to hypoxic tumor cells via DNA damage. Rationale for combining with TAE: embolization induces tumor hypoxia, potentially enhancing tirapazamine activation.

Evidence role assessment: (1) MED/35504436 - Phase I tirapazamine chemoembolization for HCC - indirect_direction, same drug/mechanism but different indication (HCC vs NET), numeric_use_allowed=false; (2) MED/34041204 - Phase I tirapazamine arterial embolization for HCC - indirect_direction, same drug/mechanism but different indication, numeric_use_allowed=false; (3) NET liver metastasis TAE studies (MED/35289113, MED/37587855) - indirect_direction, same indication but different intervention (TAE without tirapazamine), numeric_use_allowed=false.

Population matching: Current cohort is well-differentiated NET with liver-dominant metastases. Historical NET TAE studies show ORR 40-60% with TAE alone. HCC tirapazamine+TAE Phase I showed safety and some efficacy signals but no confirmed ORR data available.

Key uncertainty: No published results for tirapazamine+TAE specifically in NET population before cutoff. Phase I design primarily evaluates safety/dosing, not powered for efficacy. Expansion cohort data not available.

Safety considerations: Tirapazamine known toxicities include muscle cramps, nausea, fatigue, ototoxicity. TAE risks include post-embolization syndrome, liver dysfunction. No unexpected safety signals predicted.

Trial outcome: Likely to meet primary endpoint definition (ORR assessable) but as Phase I, success is primarily safety/tolerability with exploratory efficacy. Classification: uncertain due to lack of outcome data.

analysis_trace: Trial Identification: NCT02174549 is a Phase I dose-escalation/expansion study of intra-arterial tirapazamine combined with transarterial embolization (TAE) for liver cancer. Per the dynamic configuration, the dose-escalation (3+3) has completed, and the study is now in an expansion cohort specifically for neuroendocrine tumors (NET) with liver-dominant metastatic disease (n=25 estimated).

Patient Population: Adults (age 20-99) with well-differentiated NET and liver-dominant metastases, ECOG 0-1, Child-Pugh A, with progression on prior therapies including systemic agents, surgery, ablation, or prior transarterial therapies. This represents a heavily pretreated population.

Target Mechanism: Tirapazamine is a hypoxia-activated bioreductive prodrug that forms toxic free radicals under low oxygen conditions. Combined with TAE (which induces tumor hypoxia via Lipiodol/Gelfoam embolization), the regimen aims to achieve synergistic tumor necrosis by leveraging the hypoxic microenvironment created by embolization.

Evidence Review: Retrieved Liu et al. 2022 (PMC12483467), a Phase I study of the identical regimen (tirapazamine + TAE) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Results: 17 patients, no dose-limiting toxicities, mRECIST complete response 47%, objective response rate (ORR) 65%, median duration of response not reached at median follow-up 5.7 months, median time to progression 12.6 months.

Evidence Matching Assessment: Liu et al. provides direct evidence for the drug-dose-procedure combination but in HCC rather than NET. Evidence role: indirect_direction for efficacy (same mechanism, different tumor biology). Mismatch reason: HCC is a primary liver cancer with different vascularity and hypoxia kinetics compared to NET liver metastases; however, both are embolization-responsive liver tumors. Numeric use allowed: directional/range estimates only, not exact replication.

Evidence Role - Mechanism Background: The Liu study confirms the safety hypothesis (no DLTs at up to 20 mg/m2, Phase II dose selected at 35 mg fixed) and provides proof-of-concept that hypoxia-activation + embolization can achieve high response rates (65% mRECIST ORR in HCC). This supports mechanistic plausibility in NET.

Endpoint Interpretation - ORR by RECIST (primary-0): RECIST criteria typically yield 10-20% lower response rates than mRECIST in liver tumors due to measurement methodology. Extrapolating from 65% mRECIST in HCC, and considering NET liver metastases generally respond well to embolization (historical ORR 40-60%), predicted ORR 45% (range 25-65%).

Endpoint Interpretation - ORR by mRECIST (secondary-0): mRECIST measures viable tumor enhancement and typically shows higher response rates in HCC. Assuming similar enhancement patterns in NET liver mets and leveraging the HCC data (65% ORR), predicted mRECIST ORR 60% (range 40-75%), slightly discounted for cross-tumor uncertainty.

Endpoint Interpretation - Duration of Response (secondary-1): In HCC, median DOR was not reached at 5.7 months. For NET treated with TAE, historical median DOR ranges 6-18 months. Predicted median DOR 10 months (range 6-18 months), reflecting durable embolization effect potentially enhanced by tirapazamine-mediated hypoxic cell killing.

Safety Analysis: Liu et al. reported no DLTs or serious adverse events. Most common AEs were transient AST/ALT elevations (82.4%). This safety profile is consistent with TAE alone and suggests tirapazamine does not add significant hepatotoxicity beyond embolization. Expected safety signal: manageable transaminitis, post-embolization syndrome.

Key Risks: 1) Cross-tumor extrapolation risk: NET biology differs from HCC (slower growth, different vascularity); hypoxia-activated therapy may be less effective in NET. 2) Small sample size (n=25) limits precision of ORR estimates. 3) Prior therapy heterogeneity (some patients had prior TACE/TAE) may reduce response rates due to altered vascularity.

Evidence-to-Prediction Logic: Despite indication mismatch, the mechanism (hypoxia-activated drug + embolization) is tumor-agnostic. The high response rate in HCC (65% mRECIST) provides an upper bound; historical NET TAE data (40-60% ORR) provides a lower bound. Predictions interpolate within this range with conservative discounting.
Coverage Gaps: No published results specific to the NET cohort of NCT02174549 as of cutoff. No comparative data for tirapazamine specifically in NET. Duration of response data immature in HCC study.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC12483467 NIHMSID: NIHMS2110186 PMID: 35504436 The publisher's version of this article is available at J Vasc Interv Radiol Abstract Purpose: To investigate the safety of replacing doxorubicin with tirapazamine in conventional transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) in an Asian population with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and to determine the optimal tirapazamine dose for phase II studies. Materials and Methods: This was a phase I, 3 + 3 dose-escalation study for patients with unresectable early- and intermediate-stage HCC who received 5, 10, or 20 mg/m 2 of intra-arterial (IA) tirapazamine followed by ethiodized oil/gelatin sponge-based embolization. Key eligibilities included HCCs no more than 10 cm in diameter, prior embolization allowed, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1, Child-Pugh score of 5–7, and platelet count of ≥60,000 μL. Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was defined as any grade 3 nonhematological or grade 4 hematological toxicity, with the exception of transient elevation of aminotransferase levels after the procedure. Results: Seventeen patients were enrolled, 59% of whom had progression from a prior HCC therapy and 35% of whom had progression or recurrence after TACE. All patients tolerated the tirapazamine TACE well without any DLT or serious adverse event. Using the modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, the complete response (CR) rate was 47%, and the CR + partial response rate was 65%. The median duration of response was not reached. The median time to progression was 12.6 months (95% confidence interval, 5.1–not reached). The median overall survival was 29.3 months. The selected phase II dose was set at a fixed dose of 35 mg of IA tirapazamine. Conclusions: IA tirapazamine with transarterial embolization was well tolerated and showed promising efficacy signals in intermediate-stage HCC, justifying pursuit of a phase II study. Conventional transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is an established locoregional therapy for Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancerstage B hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ( 1 , 2 ). In this procedure, intra-arterial (IA) administration of chemotherapy (eg, doxorubicin) is performed with transarterial embolization (TAE) of the tumor-feeding arteries, which restricts oxygen supply to the tumor. However, meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials have called into question the benefits of adding chemotherapy to TAE ( 3 , 4 ). In addition, chemotherapeutic agents cannot effectively target cancer stem cells, a root cause of tumor recurrence after conventional TACE treatment, and their cytotoxic effects may be suppressed in the hypoxic environment created by embolization ( 5 - 8 ). Thus, there is a pressing unmet medical need for a new drug partner that can overcome the limitations of chemotherapy use in conventional TACE. Tirapazamine (TPZ) is a prodrug whose anticancer effects are only activated at low levels of oxygen (hypoxia). As a bioreductive agent, TPZ is converted into a toxic free radical under hypoxia but is reverted back to its inactive form when re-exposed to oxygen. Hence, free radicals accumulate only under hypoxic conditions to render cell necrosis ( 9 ). TPZ failed in several large, phase III trials in which it was administered systemically without concomitant induction of tumor hypoxia in patients with lung, cervical, or head and neck cancers ( 10 - 12 ). To address the clinical shortcomings of both conventional TACE and single-agent TPZ, a tailored TPZ chemoembolization protocol was developed. In preclinical mouse studies, TPZ combined with hepatic artery ligation yielded complete tumor necrosis in a mouse HBx transgenic model ( 13 ). In the rabbit VX2 model, Sonoda et al ( 14 ) demonstrated statistically significant tumor growth suppression with a combination of TPZ and gelatin microspheres versus either agent alone. A phase I trial ( 15 ) in unresectable treatment-naïve intermediate-stage HCC demonstrated that TPZ chemoembolization was well tolerated by patients, with no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) at 20 mg/m 2 of IA TPZ followed by embolization. This sequence of TPZ administration followed by immediate embolization was felt to be critical, using the first-pass effect of drug uptake because embolization could limit subsequent distribution of TPZ to the tumor. Moreover, in the same study ( 15 ), TPZ chemoembolization achieved a complete response (CR) rate of 60% with over a 12-month duration of CR and a median survival of 52 months. Here, the authors report a separate phase I study of TPZ chemoembolization for unresectable early- and intermediate-stage HCCs in an exclusively Asian population. This study had broader inclusion criteria, such as patients with Child-Pugh scores of 5–7 and who have previously undergone surgery, radiofrequency (RF) ablation, or embolization treatment. MATERIALS AND METHODS The regional trial was registered in Taiwan Clinical Trial Registry (#104CONS10288-Tirapazamine). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice standards. This study was a multicenter, phase I, dose-escalation, open-label study, and all participating patients signed an informed consent form before the first treatment. Patient Population Patients recruited to this trial had confirmed unresectable HCC with at least 1 tumor >10 mm and diagnostic appearance on multiphasic computed tomography (CT) or dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance (MR) imaging per the American Association for the Study of Liver Disease criteria ( 16 ). To be eligible, the largest tumor nodule had to be <10 cm in the largest diameter and the total volume of tumor could not exceed 50% of the liver. If the number of tumors was ≥5, all tumors needed to be within the same lobe. Patients were aged between 20 and 80 years; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 without known major cardiac, pulmonary, or renal dysfunction; and were candidates for embolization or conventional transarterial chemoembolization without major vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. Laboratory test requirements were an absolute neutrophil count of ≥1,500/μL, a hemoglobin level of ≥8.5 g/dL, a platelet count of ≥60,000 μL, a creatinine level of ≤2.0 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels of no more than 5-fold the upper limit of normal, and a total bilirubin level of ≤2.0 mg/dL. In terms of liver function, patients were required to have a Child-Pugh score of 5–7, prothrombin time of ≤4 seconds prolonged above the upper limit of normal, and blood oxygen saturation of ≥92% on room air. Patients who had received prior local therapies were not excluded. No therapies were administered for at least 4 weeks prior to enrollment. Patients with evidence of arterial insufficiency or microangiopathy in any organ were excluded. Patient Characteristics In the 2-year interval from September 2016 to September 2018, 24 patients were screened for the study, and 17 patients were ultimately enrolled to undergo TPZ chemoembolization procedures ( Fig 1 ). Materials and Methods: This was a phase I, 3 + 3 dose-escalation study for patients with unresectable early- and intermediate-stage HCC who received 5, 10, or 20 mg/m 2 of intra-arterial (IA) tirapazamine followed by ethiodized oil/gelatin sponge-based embolization. Key eligibilities included HCCs no more than 10 cm in diameter, prior embolization allowed, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1, Child-Pugh score of 5–7, and platelet count of ≥60,000 μL. Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was defined as any grade 3 nonhematological or grade 4 hematological toxicity, with the exception of transient elevation of aminotransferase levels after the procedure. Results: Seventeen patients were enrolled, 59% of whom had progression from a prior HCC therapy and 35% of whom had progression or recurrence after TACE. All patients tolerated the tirapazamine TACE well without any DLT or serious adverse event. Using the modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, the complete response (CR) rate was 47%, and the CR + partial response rate was 65%. The median duration of response was not reached. The median time to progression was 12.6 months (95% confidence interval, 5.1–not reached). The median overall survival was 29.3 months. The selected phase II dose was set at a fixed dose of 35 mg of IA tirapazamine. Conclusions: IA tirapazamine with transarterial embolization was well tolerated and showed promising efficacy signals in intermediate-stage HCC, justifying pursuit of a phase II study. Conventional transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is an established locoregional therapy for Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancerstage B hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ( 1 , 2 ). In this procedure, intra-arterial (IA) administration of chemotherapy (eg, doxorubicin) is performed with transarterial embolization (TAE) of the tumor-feeding arteries, which restricts oxygen supply to the tumor. However, meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials have called into question the benefits of adding chemotherapy to TAE ( 3 , 4 ). In addition, chemotherapeutic agents cannot effectively target cancer stem cells, a root cause of tumor recurrence after conventional TACE treatment, and their cytotoxic effects may be suppressed in the hypoxic environment created by embolization ( 5 - 8 ). Thus, there is a pressing unmet medical need for a new drug partner that can overcome the limitations of chemotherapy use in conventional TACE. Tirapazamine (TPZ) is a prodrug whose anticancer effects are only activated at low levels of oxygen (hypoxia). As a bioreductive agent, TPZ is converted into a toxic free radical under hypoxia but is reverted back to its inactive form when re-exposed to oxygen. Hence, free radicals accumulate only under hypoxic conditions to render cell necrosis ( 9 ). TPZ failed in several large, phase III trials in which it was administered systemically without concomitant induction of tumor hypoxia in patients with lung, cervical, or head and neck cancers ( 10 - 12 ). To address the clinical shortcomings of both conventional TACE and single-agent TPZ, a tailored TPZ chemoembolization protocol was developed. In preclinical mouse studies, TPZ combined with hepatic artery ligation yielded complete tumor necrosis in a mouse HBx transgenic model ( 13 ). In the rabbit VX2 model, Sonoda et al ( 14 ) demonstrated statistically significant tumor growth suppression with a combination of TPZ and gelatin microspheres versus either agent alone. A phase I trial ( 15 ) in unresectable treatment-naïve intermediate-stage HCC demonstrated that TPZ chemoembolization was well tolerated by patients, with no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) at 20 mg/m 2 of IA TPZ followed by embolization. This sequence of TPZ administration followed by immediate embolization was felt to be critical, using the first-pass effect of drug uptake because embolization could limit subsequent distribution of TPZ to the tumor. Moreover, in the same study ( 15 ), TPZ chemoembolization achieved a complete response (CR) rate of 60% with over a 12-month duration of CR and a median survival of 52 months. Here, the authors report a separate phase I study of TPZ chemoembolization for unresectable early- and intermediate-stage HCCs in an exclusively Asian population. This study had broader inclusion criteria, such as patients with Child-Pugh scores of 5–7 and who have previously undergone surgery, radiofrequency (RF) ablation, or embolization treatment. MATERIALS AND METHODS The regional trial was registered in Taiwan Clinical Trial Registry (#104CONS10288-Tirapazamine). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice standards. This study was a multicenter, phase I, dose-escalation, open-label study, and all participating patients signed an informed consent form before the first treatment. Patient Population Patients recruited to this trial had confirmed unresectable HCC with at least 1 tumor >10 mm and diagnostic appearance on multiphasic computed tomography (CT) or dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance (MR) imaging per the American Association for the Study of Liver Disease criteria ( 16 ). To be eligible, the largest tumor nodule had to be <10 cm in the largest diameter and the total volume of tumor could not exceed 50% of the liver. If the number of tumors was ≥5, all tumors needed to be within the same lobe. Patients were aged between 20 and 80 years; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 without known major cardiac, pulmonary, or renal dysfunction; and were candidates for embolization or conventional transarterial chemoembolization without major vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. Laboratory test requirements were an absolute neutrophil count of ≥1,500/μL, a hemoglobin level of ≥8.5 g/dL, a platelet count of ≥60,000 μL, a creatinine level of ≤2.0 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels of no more than 5-fold the upper limit of normal, and a total bilirubin level of ≤2.0 mg/dL. In terms of liver function, patients were required to have a Child-Pugh score of 5–7, prothrombin time of ≤4 seconds prolonged above the upper limit of normal, and blood oxygen saturation of ≥92% on room air. Patients who had received prior local therapies were not excluded. No therapies were administered for at least 4 weeks prior to enrollment. Patients with evidence of arterial insufficiency or microangiopathy in any organ were excluded. Patient Characteristics In the 2-year interval from September 2016 to September 2018, 24 patients were screened for the study, and 17 patients were ultimately enrolled to undergo TPZ chemoembolization procedures ( Fig 1 ). There were 3, 4, 6, and 4 patients enrolled in the 5 mg/m 2 , 10 mg/m 2 , 20 mg/m 2 , and expansion cohorts, respectively. Figure 1. Open in a new tab Study flow diagram of the phase I study. The 3 + 3 design was conducted following the standard rules. If 3 patients were enrolled without dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), the dose could be escalated to treat 3 more patients. If 1 of 3 patients in any cohort developed DLT, 3 more should be enrolled in the same cohort. If no more DLT in these 3 patients, the dose could be escalated to the next dose level. If 2 patients in any cohort developed DLT, the dose of this cohort would be considered not tolerable. Determination of the selected phase II dose was based on 6 patients without DLT in the 20 mg/m 2 cohort. HCC = hepatocellular carcinoma. The demographics of the 17 patients are shown in Table 1 . Ten patients had received prior therapy for HCC, such as surgery, RF ablation, or TACE. Study Design The study was designed as a classic 3 + 3 dose-escalation study ( 17 ). TPZ (Teclison, Princeton, New Jersey) was provided in citrate buffer (pH, 4) at 0.7 mg/mL and was injected directly without dilution. Patients received IA TPZ and then underwent embolization first with injections of ethiodized oil (Lipiodol; Guerbet, Villepinte, France) and subsequently gelatin sponge cube slurry (<1 mm in size) (Surgifoam; Ethicon, Somerville, New Jersey) mixed with a contrast medium. The goal was to achieve TPZ saturation within the HCC tumors and then induce hypoxia through embolization to activate TPZ. The initial dose of TPZ was 5 mg/m 2 , administered intra-arterially at a rate of 6 mL/min, and was increased to 10 and 20 mg/m 2 . In the expansion cohort, the dose of 20 mg/m 2 (administered intra-arterially) was converted to a fixed IA dose of 35 mg or 50 mL over 8–9 minutes, similar to what was used in a previous trial ( 15 ). The dose could be divided into up to 4 aliquots if >1 tumor was treated. Moderate sedation or general anesthesia was used for infusion-related pain control during the procedure. Cone-beam CT (Philips or Siemens per site availability) with navigation software was used to facilitate the identification of tumor-feeding arteries ( 18 , 19 ). After complete administration of the TPZ dose, straight ethiodized oil was injected within 5 minutes under fluoroscopic guidance until stasis. The total volume of ethiodized oil was generally <10 mL unless a large tumor >6 cm in diameter was treated. Gelatin sponge was cut into 1 mm cubes and mixed with contrast medium and injected immediately after the ethiodized oil until reflux was observed on fluoroscopic imaging and no further contrast medium could be injected after a 3-minute wait. Cone-beam CT was performed to ensure complete ethiodized oil coverage, meaning that the entire tumor showed uptake of ethiodized oil. After the procedure was completed, all patients were admitted for 2–3 days until the elevated AST/ALT levels showed a downward trend. Outpatient clinical visits, including complete blood count, chemistry, and α-fetoprotein tests, were conducted on days 8, 15, and 43. DLT was fully assessed at the day 15 visit to determine if patients were free of DLT. The frequency of TPZ chemoembolization was determined by the “on-demand” mode, and the investigator determined the need for subsequent TPZ chemoembolization procedures on the basis of the response, presence of residual viable tumor, and tolerability. No other therapeutic modalities were allowed during the study. Investigators could stop TPZ chemoembolization treatment and withdraw patients from the study if patients did not achieve CR, had treatment-related toxicity, or were to receive other therapeutic interventions (eg, RF ablation, conventional transarterial chemoembolization, or surgery). Study Endpoints The primary endpoint of the study was to evaluate the safety and tolerability of TPZ chemoembolization in patients with unresectable early- and intermediate-stage HCC. DLT was defined as any grade ≥3 nonhematological or grade ≥4 hematological toxicity within 15 days after the initial therapy. Persistent postembolization AST/ALT/total bilirubin levels of ≥1.5-fold baseline or ≥1.5-fold the upper normal limit without recovery within 15 days were counted as DLT. analysis_trace: Trial Identification: NCT02174549 is a Phase I dose-escalation/expansion study of intra-arterial tirapazamine combined with transarterial embolization (TAE) for liver cancer. Per the dynamic configuration, the dose-escalation (3+3) has completed, and the study is now in an expansion cohort specifically for neuroendocrine tumors (NET) with liver-dominant metastatic disease (n=25 estimated).

Patient Population: Adults (age 20-99) with well-differentiated NET and liver-dominant metastases, ECOG 0-1, Child-Pugh A, with progression on prior therapies including systemic agents, surgery, ablation, or prior transarterial therapies. This represents a heavily pretreated population.

Target Mechanism: Tirapazamine is a hypoxia-activated bioreductive prodrug that forms toxic free radicals under low oxygen conditions. Combined with TAE (which induces tumor hypoxia via Lipiodol/Gelfoam embolization), the regimen aims to achieve synergistic tumor necrosis by leveraging the hypoxic microenvironment created by embolization.

Evidence Review: Retrieved Liu et al. 2022 (PMC12483467), a Phase I study of the identical regimen (tirapazamine + TAE) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Results: 17 patients, no dose-limiting toxicities, mRECIST complete response 47%, objective response rate (ORR) 65%, median duration of response not reached at median follow-up 5.7 months, median time to progression 12.6 months.

Evidence Matching Assessment: Liu et al. provides direct evidence for the drug-dose-procedure combination but in HCC rather than NET. Evidence role: indirect_direction for efficacy (same mechanism, different tumor biology). Mismatch reason: HCC is a primary liver cancer with different vascularity and hypoxia kinetics compared to NET liver metastases; however, both are embolization-responsive liver tumors. Numeric use allowed: directional/range estimates only, not exact replication.

Evidence Role - Mechanism Background: The Liu study confirms the safety hypothesis (no DLTs at up to 20 mg/m2, Phase II dose selected at 35 mg fixed) and provides proof-of-concept that hypoxia-activation + embolization can achieve high response rates (65% mRECIST ORR in HCC). This supports mechanistic plausibility in NET.

Endpoint Interpretation - ORR by RECIST (primary-0): RECIST criteria typically yield 10-20% lower response rates than mRECIST in liver tumors due to measurement methodology. Extrapolating from 65% mRECIST in HCC, and considering NET liver metastases generally respond well to embolization (historical ORR 40-60%), predicted ORR 45% (range 25-65%).

Endpoint Interpretation - ORR by mRECIST (secondary-0): mRECIST measures viable tumor enhancement and typically shows higher response rates in HCC. Assuming similar enhancement patterns in NET liver mets and leveraging the HCC data (65% ORR), predicted mRECIST ORR 60% (range 40-75%), slightly discounted for cross-tumor uncertainty.

Endpoint Interpretation - Duration of Response (secondary-1): In HCC, median DOR was not reached at 5.7 months. For NET treated with TAE, historical median DOR ranges 6-18 months. Predicted median DOR 10 months (range 6-18 months), reflecting durable embolization effect potentially enhanced by tirapazamine-mediated hypoxic cell killing.

Safety Analysis: Liu et al. reported no DLTs or serious adverse events. Most common AEs were transient AST/ALT elevations (82.4%). This safety profile is consistent with TAE alone and suggests tirapazamine does not add significant hepatotoxicity beyond embolization. Expected safety signal: manageable transaminitis, post-embolization syndrome.

Key Risks: 1) Cross-tumor extrapolation risk: NET biology differs from HCC (slower growth, different vascularity); hypoxia-activated therapy may be less effective in NET. 2) Small sample size (n=25) limits precision of ORR estimates. 3) Prior therapy heterogeneity (some patients had prior TACE/TAE) may reduce response rates due to altered vascularity.

Evidence-to-Prediction Logic: Despite indication mismatch, the mechanism (hypoxia-activated drug + embolization) is tumor-agnostic.
